lines: Across UX Labs studies, maps had a sixty-eight percent click rate.
Travelers plan on maps. They check what's close, and whether a day is even possible.
On Bing, planning a trip meant switching between apps and sites for hotels, flights, activities and transit.
There was no way to narrow the map to what mattered, and little help deciding where to go at all.
Many travelers start without a destination, so the map starts there too.
It groups places by continent, offers trips nearby priced from where you're browsing, and themes like beaches or adventure narrow the field.
Then I brought every travel vertical onto a single map.
One search covers destinations, hotels and attractions, and the map pins all of them, so a hotel's distance from the sights shows at a glance.
But a map with every pin is as hard to read as a long list.
So filters narrow it to attractions, stays or restaurants, where a heat map shows demand, and transit shows how to get around.
I explored the map from mild to wild. The mild ideas gave engineering something to build early, and the wild ones showed where it could go.
Then I tested the concepts with users, prioritized an MVP with product and engineering, and delivered its key modules.
Design without constraints first, then let the team decide what ships.
